newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian Islamist hails French hands-off policy.
newsitem.headline: Algerian Islamist hails French hands-off policy.

text.p: Algeria's main legal Moslem fundamentalist party leader has welcomed the French government's stated policy to keep from interfering in Algeria's civil strife.

"France's position to abstain from meddling in Algerian internal affairs and respect Algeria's sovereignty is contrary to the European Parliament which is trying to intervene in the country's constitutional and internal affairs," said Hamas leader Mahfoud Nahnah.

Late in January, the French government rebuffed calls for a political initiative on Algeria's crisis, reasserting that the North African country -- its former colony -- is an independent state and it is the responsibility of the Algerian people and leaders to find solution.

Nahnah, quoted on Monday by the London-based Arab newspaper al Hayat, also assailed a new political party set up by President Liamine Zeroual's staunch supporters, describing it as a government "Trojan horse" to dominate the political field.

Nahnah gained one third of the vote in 1995 presidential elections won by Zeroual and his Hamas party was tipped by Algerian pundits to play a prominent role in the country's parliamentary elections planned for this summer.
Zeroual's close allies announced late in February the creation of a political party, called the National Democratic Rally (NDR), ahead of the poll.
The NDR party is headed by Abdelkader Bensalah, president of the government-appointed Transitional National Council, a quasi parliament.
Algeria has been without a parliament since the authorities cancelled a general election in 1992 in which radical Islamists had taken a commanding lead.
Scrapping the poll plunged Algeria into a five-year-old civil strife pitting Moslem guerrillas against government forces in which about 60,000 people have died.
